paras: The resignation of mail clerk I. Bowman at Mansura, Louisiana, took place in August 1903, when Bowman, a Black railway mail clerk in Avoyelles parish, quit after what he described as threats from a mob at Mansura. He gave up his post, saying it would be dangerous to remain in the service. Within a day the town marshal of Mansura denied the account, saying that he was the "mob" and that Bowman had fled an arrest.

Bowman was from Hamburg, Louisiana, and worked as a mail clerk on the Simmesport and Bunkie Railroad in Avoyelles parish. According to the New Orleans dispatch that first reported the case, "ill-feeling" had existed in the parish for some time over the employment of Black mail clerks.

The coverage gives no date or detail for the encounter at Mansura itself. In a dispatch dated August 23, Bowman was reported to have resigned because a mob at Mansura had threatened him. A differently worded wire item printed in Mississippi said he alleged that he had been "threatened with death." He also reported to the postal authorities that a mob had attacked him.

On August 24, D. M. Lemoine, the town marshal of Mansura, denied Bowman's story. Lemoine said that Bowman had assaulted a white boy and drawn a pistol on him, and that when he tried to arrest Bowman as an officer of the law, Bowman fled. A Louisiana paper later noted only that it was "denied at Mansura" that a mob had forced the clerk to resign. No report of an arrest, charge or postal investigation appears in the coverage.

The story reached readers through brief wire items from New Orleans. The New York Sun carried both sides on successive days, first under the headline "Negro Mall [Mail] Clerk Resigns Because Threatened by a Mob" and then under "Negro's Tale of Mob Attack Denied," a follow-up that gave the marshal's version without comment. The Sun's first item was also the only one to mention local hostility to Black mail clerks.

Elsewhere the case shrank to a single line in news digests. The Minneapolis Journal ran it on August 24 in its "Told in a Line" column, and the same sentence appeared over the next ten days in weeklies in Wisconsin and South Dakota, one of which printed the name as "L. Bowman." Vermont weeklies reduced it further to "Negro mail clerk in Louisiana resigns, fearing mob." Mississippi weeklies printed the "threatened with death" version. Only the Sun and the New Iberia paper in Louisiana printed the denial, and none of the digests found carried it. No Black-press coverage of the case was found.

Two versions of the episode appeared. In Bowman's account, relayed by wire, a mob at Mansura threatened him and he resigned in fear for his safety. In the account of Marshal Lemoine, who said he was himself the man Bowman fled, there was no mob, only an attempted arrest for an alleged assault on a white boy. Neither account was tested by any inquiry reported in the coverage.

accounts.label: Bowman's account (wire report)
accounts.gist: Bowman said a mob at Mansura threatened him and that it would be dangerous to stay in the service, so he resigned; one version says he was threatened with death.

accounts.label: Town marshal's claim
accounts.gist: Marshal Lemoine said there was no mob: Bowman had assaulted a white boy and drawn a pistol, and when Lemoine tried to arrest him he fled and told the postal authorities a mob had attacked him.

framing.detail: The Sun headed the first story 'Negro Mall [Mail] Clerk Resigns Because Threatened by a Mob' and added that ill-feeling over Black mail clerks had long existed in the parish.
The Sun's follow-up, 'Negro's Tale of Mob Attack Denied,' gave the marshal's version without comment, calling Bowman's account a 'story' and a 'tale'.
Midwestern and Vermont weeklies ran one-line digest items repeating Bowman's version without the denial.
The New Iberia paper, in Louisiana, printed only the denial.
